newsitem.title: FINLAND: FINNISH EMU DEBT SEEN BELOW 60 PCT 1997 - MINISTRY.
newsitem.headline: FINNISH EMU DEBT SEEN BELOW 60 PCT 1997 - MINISTRY.

text.p: Finland's gross public debt looks like falling below 60 percent of gross domestic product in 1997 and so meet the debt criterion for Economic and Monetary Union, a senior finance ministry official said on Friday.

"It looks like we will be going below 60 percent," the official said. He spoke on condition of anonymity, pointing out that the ministry had not yet formally revised its forecasts for how Finland will meet the EMU entry criteria in 1997.
"The debt trend has been more favourable than expected," he said.
The official's claim of a more favourable trend in the state's borrowing need was supported by this year's third supplementary budget, due to be passed to parliament on Friday.

The extra draft budget contains no new expenditure, but only increases in revenue -- 1.46 billion markka -- stemming from the state's sale of shares in chemicals group Kemira Oy and in data services group TT Tieto Oy .
Net borrowing will be reduced by the corresponding amount, and total 1996 net borrowing will fall to 37.5 billion markka from 39 billion projected earlier.
According to the finance ministry's September forecast, Finnish gross public debt to GDP would fall to 61.0 percent in 1997 from 61.8 percent this year.
That forecast was based on an acceleration in GDP growth to 3.9 percent in 1997 from 2.8 percent this year.

The ministry's new projection for the so called EMU debt was not based on any dramatic improvement in the state finances, but rather on a trend seen in domestic work pension funds' investments in government bonds, the official said.
"It is even possible that they would gobble up the whole amount of our (the state's) new 1997 net borrowing," he said.

In that case, gross public debt to GDP would fall even more, he added. Work pension funds' holdings of state paper are reduced from the total outstanding debt when calculating the EMU debt to GDP ratio.
Arto Ojala, managing director of the Federation of Finnish Insurance Companies, told a seminar late on Thursday evening that the gross public debt to GDP figure was heading for 58 percent in 1997.
By pushing debt to GDP below 60 percent next year, Finland would formally meet four of five criteria for membership of the third phase of Economic and Monetary Union.

Finland handily meets the criteria for inflation and long-term interest rates. The public sector deficit to GDP ratio is forecast by the finance ministry to fall to 1.4 percent in 1997 from 2.9 percent this year. The limit is three percent.
The Finnish markka was pegged to Europe's exchange rate mechanism ERM in October.
The third phase of EMU is scheduled to begin in January 1999. The Finnish government's stated objective is that Finland should be in the first group of countries establishing a single currency block.
